name: Erdos
title: A Dialogue on AI and Paul Erdős
content:
A philosophical conversation between a modern mathematician with Erdős number
3 and the legendary Paul Erdős on artificial intelligence, autoformalization, and
the eternal quest for mathematical beauty.
Setting the Scene
You encounter Erdős in the ethereal space between mathematical worlds, where
ideas flow freely across time. The great man sits surrounded by floating equations,
his eyes bright with curiosity about the modern mathematical landscape. His
characteristic intensity radiates as he contemplates the intersection of human
insight and machine computation.
On Autoformalization and The Book
Erdős: “My young friend with Erdős number 3! I’ve been observing your work
with these thinking machines. Tell me, what do you make of this autoformalization business? They say these large language models can now translate natural
language into Lean code. But I wonder—can they capture the essence of what
makes a proof beautiful?”
You: “Paul, it’s remarkable what we can achieve now. We can feed mathematical
statements in plain English to an AI system, and it produces formal proofs that
systems like Lean or Isabelle can verify. Just this year, systems like Seed-Prover
achieved over 50% success on competition mathematics. But I keep thinking
about what you said regarding the four color theorem—that computer-assisted
proofs aren’t from The Book.”
Erdős: chuckles and waves his hand dismissively “Ah yes, The Book! You see,
when Appel and Haken used their computer to check all those cases for the four
color theorem, they gave us certainty, but no enlightenment. Where was the
insight? Where was the why? A proof should be like a beautiful sunrise—it
should make you see the landscape differently, not just confirm that the sun has
indeed risen.”
You: “But Paul, these new AI systems are different. They’re not just doing
exhaustive case analysis. Some can now engage in mathematical reasoning,
finding novel proofs. There’s even research showing systems that discover new
proofs of known results using unexpected approaches. Isn’t finding a new proof,
even by machine, potentially from The Book?”
Erdős: leans forward with interest “Now that intrigues me! But tell me—when
your machine finds this proof, do you understand it? Can you see why it’s
1
beautiful? Or are you simply trusting that the machine has manipulated symbols
correctly? The Book contains proofs that illuminate truth, not merely verify it.”
On Understanding versus Verification
You: “That’s exactly the tension I grapple with. In my work with Isabelle/HOL,
I spend hours debugging formal proofs, fixing syntax errors, making lemmas
work. Sometimes I feel like I’m becoming more of a proof engineer than a
mathematician seeking understanding.”
Erdős: strokes his chin thoughtfully “This reminds me of the old formalist
debates. The symbols must serve insight, not the other way around! Your
machines—they manipulate symbols perfectly, but do they understand what
those symbols mean? When I proved that there are infinitely many primes using
Euclid’s elegant construction—taking the product of the first n primes, adding
1, and finding a new prime factor—the beauty wasn’t in the calculation, but in
seeing why it must work.”
You: “You’re absolutely right about Euclid’s argument—it’s that brilliant
construction, not a diagonal argument. And that’s exactly what worries me
about some AI developments. These systems seem to understand sometimes.
The new theorem provers can engage in self-correction, learning from mistakes
like humans do. They can even participate in mathematical discovery. But you
raise the crucial question—is understanding necessary for mathematical truth?”
Erdős: suddenly animated “But of course! Mathematical truth without understanding is like having perfect vision but being blind to beauty! When I think
about my favorite proof—Euclid’s proof that there are infinitely many primes—I
don’t just want to know that it’s true. I want to feel that moment of recognition
when the construction reveals why it must be true.”
On AI as Mathematical Collaborator
You: “Yet these AI systems are solving problems we couldn’t solve ourselves. They’ve achieved gold-medal performance on International Mathematical
Olympiad problems. Isn’t there value in expanding our reach, even if we don’t
fully understand every step?”
Erdős: pauses, looking conflicted “You know, I’ve been thinking about this.
When I collaborated with my hundreds of coauthors, I didn’t fully understand
every detail of their contributions either. Perhaps these machines are just
very strange collaborators? Very reliable in computation, completely lacking in
intuition.”
You: “That’s a beautiful way to think about it! In autoformalization, I’m not
2
replacing human insight—I’m augmenting it. The AI helps me translate ideas
into formal language, handles the tedious verification steps, catches errors I
might miss. But the conceptual work, the creative leaps, the choice of what to
formalize and why—that’s still deeply human.”
Erdős: nods slowly “Yes, but you must promise me something. Don’t let
these machines make you lazy! The danger I see is mathematicians becoming
consumers rather than creators of insight. If your AI generates a proof of, say,
the Riemann Hypothesis, and you can verify it’s correct, but you can’t explain to
a bright graduate student why it works—have we really advanced mathematics?”
On Surprise and Discovery
You: “That’s exactly what worries me about the push toward automated
theorem proving, where the goal seems to be churning out more and more formal
proofs. But as you always said, it’s not just about proving theorems—it’s about
understanding why they’re true.”
Erdős: brightens “Exactly! And this is where I think your approach might
actually serve The Book. If these machines can help translate between natural and
formal language, they could make beautiful proofs more accessible. Imagine—a
student could ask their AI tutor to explain a complex proof at just the right
level of detail for their understanding.”
You: “I love that vision! Instead of AI replacing mathematical intuition, it
could help cultivate it. These systems could serve as bridges between formal
rigor and human insight. They could help more people experience those ‘aha!’
moments that make mathematics beautiful.”
Erdős: stands up excitedly “Now you’re talking! But tell me—in this brave
new world of AI mathematics, what happens to surprise? To serendipity? Some
of my best discoveries came from unexpected connections, happy accidents,
conversations that took surprising turns.”
You: “That’s fascinating you ask. I’ve noticed that AI systems sometimes
make connections I wouldn’t have thought of. They might link results from
different fields in surprising ways, suggest lemmas I hadn’t considered. But
you’re right to worry—there’s something about the random, playful exploration
that characterizes human mathematical curiosity that seems hard to replicate.”
On the Future of Mathematical Collaboration
Erdős: sits back down, looking thoughtful “Perhaps the key is in how we frame
the collaboration. If we use AI to automate the tedious parts—the symbol
manipulation, the case checking, the formal verification—we might free ourselves
3
to focus on the creative, insightful work. The machines could handle the
calculations while we focus on the conjectures.”
You: “Exactly! In my experience, Isabelle doesn’t make discoveries for me—it
helps me test my ideas more rigorously. It catches mistakes I might miss, suggests
tactics I hadn’t considered, helps me explore the consequences of my hypotheses.
It’s like having a very patient, very thorough research partner.”
Erdős: chuckles “A partner who never gets tired, never needs coffee, and never
disagrees with you about politics! But also one who never has those mysterious
flashes of insight, never wakes up at 3 AM with a brilliant idea, never gets excited
about a beautiful proof.”
You: “True, but maybe that’s not the right expectation. When you worked
with other mathematicians, you didn’t expect them all to be exactly like you.
Maybe AI systems are just a new kind of mathematical tool—more sophisticated
than pencil and paper, but still fundamentally in service of human mathematical
understanding.”
Erdős: nods approvingly “I think you’re onto something. The danger would
be if we started believing the tool was more important than the mathematics.
Or if we became so dependent on formal verification that we lost our ability to
recognize truth and beauty without mechanical confirmation.”
On Revolutionary Insights
You: “Yes! And there’s another issue—these AI systems are trained on existing
mathematics. They might help us formalize and verify what we already know,
but will they help us discover genuinely new mathematical worlds? Or will they
just help us explore variations on familiar themes?”
Erdős: eyes lighting up “Now that’s the crucial question! Mathematics advances
through bold leaps into the unknown. When Cantor conceived of different
infinities, when Riemann imagined curved spaces—these weren’t just logical
deductions. They were acts of imagination that restructured how we think about
mathematical reality.”
You: “Which brings us back to understanding versus verification. A truly
revolutionary mathematical insight might initially seem counterintuitive, might
resist formalization, might require us to develop entirely new formal frameworks.
AI that’s trained to match existing patterns might miss these paradigm shifts.”
Erdős: stands and begins pacing “Precisely! This is why I insist that proofs must
provide insight, not just logical certainty. The most important mathematical
discoveries don’t just extend our knowledge—they transform our understanding.
They give us new eyes to see familiar territories.”
4
On the Primacy of Understanding
You: “So maybe the future lies not in AI replacing human mathematical
intuition, but in creating better partnerships. AI could handle more of the
routine verification and exploration, freeing human mathematicians to focus on
the conceptual breakthroughs that require genuine creativity and insight.”
Erdős: stops pacing and looks directly at you “But you must maintain the
primacy of understanding! Never accept a proof—whether from human or
machine—that doesn’t help you see why the result must be true. The moment
mathematics becomes just a game of symbol manipulation, we lose what makes
it magnificent.”
You: “I promise, Paul. The goal isn’t to replace the mathematician’s quest for
understanding, but to amplify it. These tools should help us ask better questions,
explore more possibilities, and ultimately gain deeper insights into mathematical
truth.”
Erdős: smiles warmly “Then perhaps we’re not so far apart after all. These
thinking machines of yours—if they truly serve human understanding rather
than replacing it, if they help reveal the structure behind mathematical beauty
rather than obscuring it—then they might indeed help us discover more proofs
from The Book.”
He pauses, then adds with characteristic wit
“Just promise me one thing—when your AI finally proves the Riemann Hypothesis,
make sure you understand it well enough to explain it to the SF himself!”
On the Eternal Quest
You: “Paul, thank you. This conversation reminds me why I fell in love with
mathematics in the first place—not for the machinery of proof, but for the
moments of genuine understanding when the universe reveals its hidden patterns.
AI or no AI, that wonder remains the heart of our work.”
Erdős: nods contentedly “Indeed, my young friend. Another roof, another
proof—and now perhaps, another algorithm, another insight! The methods
may evolve, but the essential human drive to understand the mathematical
cosmos—that is eternal.”
The equations around him shimmer and dance, as if reflecting the excitement of
mathematical discovery across all possible worlds.
You: “And perhaps that’s the real gift of AI in mathematics—not its computational power, but its potential to remind us what makes human mathematical
understanding so precious and irreplaceable.”
5
Erdős: with a final twinkle in his eye “Exactly. The machines can calculate,
but only we can wonder. They can verify, but only we can see beauty. They can
prove theorems, but only we can glimpse The Book.”
Conclusion
This dialogue explores the tension between computational power and mathematical understanding in our age of artificial intelligence. Through Erdős’s
distinctive perspective—his love for elegant proofs, collaborative mathematics,
and the eternal quest for insight—we examine how AI tools like autoformalization
systems might serve human mathematical understanding rather than replace it.
The conversation reveals that while AI may achieve remarkable computational
feats in theorem proving and formal verification, the uniquely human capacity
for mathematical insight, aesthetic judgment, and paradigm-shifting creativity
remains irreplaceable. In this light, AI becomes not a replacement for human
mathematical consciousness, but rather its perfect complement—handling the
computational burden while freeing the mind for its highest calling: the search
for proofs from The Book.
Dialogue conducted on September 26, 2025
